subject: DI02000021

intro_text.en: Unit 1 of Engineering Mathematics: what a matrix is and how it is written, the types you must recognise, addition, subtraction and scalar multiplication, the row-into-column product with its size rule, the adjoint and inverse of 2 × 2 and 3 × 3 matrices, and the solution of two simultaneous equations by the inverse-matrix method and by Cramer's rule. Twenty-four fully solved numericals, each linked to a card.

h.en: 1.1 Order, entries and the meaning of aᵢⱼ

body.en:
Definition

A matrix is a rectangular arrangement of numbers written inside brackets. The numbers inside are called elements or entries. A matrix has no value of its own: it is an array, so it is never equal to a single number.

A matrix with m rows and n columns has order m × n. The entry in row i and column j is written aᵢⱼ - the row number always comes first.

Counting the entries

  • A 2 × 3 matrix has 2 × 3 = 6 entries.
  • A 3 × 3 matrix has 9 entries and is called square.
  • a₂₃ means row 2, column 3 - not row 3, column 2.

Worked reading

For A =
2−13
054
the order is 2 × 3, so a₁₃ = 3 and a₂₂ = 5. There is no a₃₁: the matrix has only two rows.

Common mistake

Writing the order as 3 × 2 because three columns are visible. Read rows first: count the horizontal lines, then the vertical ones.

h.en: 1.2 Building a matrix from a rule, and equality

body.en:
Definition

A matrix may be described by a formula for its general entry, for example aᵢⱼ = 2i + j for a 2 × 3 matrix. Substitute every (i, j) pair in turn.

Worked example

a₁₁ = 2(1) + 1 = 3, a₁₂ = 4, a₁₃ = 5, a₂₁ = 5, a₂₂ = 6, a₂₃ = 7, so the matrix is
345
567
.

When two matrices are equal

  • The orders must be identical, and
  • every pair of matching entries must be equal.

So
x + 13
2y − 2
=
53
24
gives x + 1 = 5 and y − 2 = 4, that is x = 4 and y = 6.

Can a 2 × 2 matrix equal a 2 × 3 matrix?

Never. Equality starts with the order; different orders mean different arrays.

h.en: 1.3 The transpose of a matrix

body.en:
Definition

The transpose Aᵀ is made by turning rows into columns: the first row of A becomes the first column of Aᵀ. A 2 × 3 matrix has a 3 × 2 transpose.

Worked example

A =
123
456
gives Aᵀ =
14
25
36
, and transposing again returns A: (Aᵀ)ᵀ = A.

Rules

  • (Aᵀ)ᵀ = A
  • (A + B)ᵀ = Aᵀ + Bᵀ
  • (kA)ᵀ = kAᵀ
  • (AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ - the order reverses, as it does for inverses.

A square matrix that equals its own transpose is symmetric.

h.en: 1.4 Why engineers use matrices

body.en:
Where matrices appear

  • A network of currents or forces is written as one matrix of coefficients - one row per equation.
  • A transformation (rotation, scaling, mirror) is stored as a 2 × 2 matrix, and multiplying it by a position vector gives the new position.
  • A spreadsheet, a digital photograph and a table of readings are all matrices: row and column positions locate each number.

The three questions this unit answers

  1. How do I add and multiply these arrays?
  2. How do I undo a square matrix (the inverse)?
  3. How do I read the solution of two equations straight out of the matrices?

Everything later in the semester - differentiation, integration, differential equations - is built on these three skills.

h.en: 2.1 Square, diagonal, scalar, identity and zero matrices

body.en:
Definitions

  • Square: number of rows equals number of columns (2 × 2, 3 × 3).
  • Diagonal: square, and every entry off the main diagonal is zero.
  • Scalar: a diagonal matrix whose diagonal entries are all equal.
  • Identity I: a scalar matrix with 1 on the diagonal - the matrix version of the number 1.
  • Zero matrix O: every entry is 0 - the matrix version of 0.

Why the identity matters

AI = IA = A for every matrix A that can be multiplied with I. It is the reason a matrix can have an inverse at all: A⁻¹ is defined by A A⁻¹ = I.

Reading the diagram

Each panel shows the pattern only. A diagonal matrix may have any numbers on its diagonal - what makes it diagonal is the ring of zeros everywhere else.

h.en: 2.2 Row, column, rectangular and triangular matrices

body.en:
Definitions

  • Row matrix: a single row (order 1 × n).
  • Column matrix (column vector): a single column (order m × 1).
  • Rectangular: rows ≠ columns.
  • Upper triangular: square, every entry below the main diagonal is zero.
  • Lower triangular: square, every entry above the main diagonal is zero.

Worked reading

27
04
is upper triangular and
20
54
is lower triangular. A matrix can be both only if it is diagonal.

Useful fact

The determinant of a triangular matrix is simply the product of its diagonal entries, so |
27
04
| = 2 × 4 = 8 - no expansion needed.

A row matrix is the same idea as a vector, so Unit 3 of semester 1 (vectors) and this unit speak the same language.

h.en: 2.3 Symmetric and skew-symmetric matrices

body.en:
Definitions

  • Symmetric: Aᵀ = A, so aᵢⱼ = aⱼᵢ - the entries mirror across the main diagonal.
  • Skew-symmetric: Aᵀ = −A, so aᵢⱼ = −aⱼᵢ and every diagonal entry must be 0.

A construction that always works

For any square matrix A, the sum A + Aᵀ is symmetric and the difference A − Aᵀ is skew-symmetric. Check: (A + Aᵀ)ᵀ = Aᵀ + A = A + Aᵀ.

Worked example

A =
12
34
gives Aᵀ =
13
24
and A + Aᵀ =
25
58
, which is symmetric because 5 = 5 across the diagonal.

Symmetric matrices appear wherever a quantity is measured in both directions: a distance table, a stiffness matrix, a correlation table.

h.en: 2.4 Singular and non-singular matrices

body.en:
Definitions

  • Non-singular: |A| ≠ 0. The matrix has an inverse.
  • Singular: |A| = 0. No inverse exists.

Why the determinant decides

The inverse formula is A⁻¹ = adj A ÷ |A|. If |A| = 0 the division is impossible, so the inverse does not exist - it is not that the answer is zero, it is that there is no answer.

The geometric reading

Two equations with determinant 0 have proportional rows, so their lines are parallel (no solution) or identical (infinitely many). A matrix with an inverse always gives exactly one solution.

Common mistake

Writing A⁻¹ = 1/|A| without the adjoint. The determinant is a number, the adjoint is a matrix, and the inverse is the adjoint scaled by that number.

h.en: 3.1 Adding and subtracting matrices

body.en:
Rule

Two matrices can be added or subtracted only when they have the same order. The answer keeps that order and each entry is added or subtracted separately: Cᵢⱼ = aᵢⱼ ± bᵢⱼ.

Worked example

A =
123
456
and B =
654
321
give A + B =
777
777
and A − B =
−5−3−1
135
.

Laws

  • A + B = B + A (addition commutes)
  • A + (B + C) = (A + B) + C (associates)
  • A + O = A, and A + (−A) = O

So the change B − A is not the same matrix as A − B: subtraction reverses every sign.

h.en: 3.2 Multiplication by a scalar

body.en:
Rule

A scalar is a single number. Multiply every entry: (kA)ᵢⱼ = k aᵢⱼ. The order does not change.

Worked example

4A with A =
1/23
−11/4
gives
212
−41
.

Laws

  • k(A + B) = kA + kB
  • (k + m)A = kA + mA
  • k(mA) = (km)A
  • 1A = A and 0A = O

Common mistake

Scaling only the first row or only the diagonal. A scalar multiplies every entry, which is exactly why kA ≠ A for most matrices - and why 2I is not the identity.

h.en: 3.3 Mixed expressions such as 3A − 2B

body.en:
Method

  1. Work out 3A on its own.
  2. Work out 2B on its own.
  3. Subtract entry by entry, keeping the order of the two matrices.

Worked example

A =
2−1
30
and B =
14
−25
: 3A =
6−3
90
, 2B =
28
−410
, so 3A − 2B =
4−11
13−10

Conditions

  • Both matrices must have the same order.
  • There is no matrix division: never write 3A/2B.
  • A scalar outside the bracket multiplies every entry inside it.

This is the sort of expression that appears when you compute A² − 3A + 2I in the next section.

h.en: 3.4 Checking your arithmetic

body.en:
Three quick checks

  1. Order check: both input matrices and the answer must carry the same order.
  2. Sign check: in a subtraction, the second matrix reverses every one of its signs.
  3. Corner check: recompute the top-left and the bottom-right entries by hand; if either disagrees, the whole matrix is suspect.

Why it matters later

The same three checks catch errors in AB, in the adjoint and in Cramer's rule. Almost every lost mark in a matrices question is an arithmetic slip in one entry, not a wrong method.

Keep the working as a matrix - write the unsimplified sum first, then simplify in a second line. That way the marker can see the method even if one entry is wrong.

h.en: 4.1 Row into column: the definition of AB

body.en:
Definition

The product AB exists only when the number of columns of A equals the number of rows of B. The answer then has the rows of A and the columns of B: an m × n matrix times an n × p matrix gives an m × p matrix.

Each entry is a row-times-column sum: (AB)ᵢⱼ = aᵢ₁b₁ⱼ + aᵢ₂b₂ⱼ + ... + aᵢₙbₙⱼ.

Step by step

  1. Take row i of A and column j of B.
  2. Multiply the first pair, the second pair, and so on.
  3. Add the products - that single number is the (i, j) entry of AB.

Worked example

A =
12
34
and B =
20
13
give AB =
46
1012
: the top-left entry is 1(2) + 2(1) = 4 and the bottom-right is 3(0) + 4(3) = 12.

h.en: 4.2 AB is usually not BA

body.en:
The rule

Matrix multiplication is not commutative: AB ≠ BA in general. Often both products exist but they are different matrices; sometimes only one of them can be formed at all.

Worked comparison

With A =
12
34
and B =
20
13
, AB =
46
1012
but BA =
24
1014
. Same order, different entries.

What does survive

  • (AB)C = A(BC) - multiplication is associative.
  • A(B + C) = AB + AC - it distributes over addition.
  • (AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ and (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹ - both reverse the order.

Common mistake

Swapping AB for BA to make the answer look nicer. In a transformation problem that changes the physical meaning: rotate-then-scale is not scale-then-rotate.

h.en: 4.3 Checking conformability before you multiply

body.en:
The size test

Write the two orders side by side and cross out the inner numbers: (m × n)(n × p) = m × p. If the inner numbers differ, the product does not exist - no working, no marks.

Examples of the test

ProductInner numbersResult
(2 × 3)(3 × 2)3 and 3 - match2 × 2
(3 × 2)(2 × 4)2 and 2 - match3 × 4
(2 × 3)(2 × 3)3 and 2 - differnot defined

Worked example

A =
123
456

10

is 3 × 2, so AB exists and is 2 × 2: AB =
511
1423
.

Note that BA would be 3 × 3 - a different size entirely. The two products cannot be compared entry by entry.

h.en: 4.4 Powers of a matrix and matrix polynomials

body.en:
Definition

A² means A × A, so it exists only for a square matrix. The expression A² − 3A + 2I is evaluated term by term: a matrix minus a matrix plus a matrix, where 2I is not the number 2.

Worked example

A =
21
10
: A² =
52
21
, 3A =
63
30
, 2I =
20
02
, so A² − 3A + 2I =
1−1
−13
.

The trap

Filling the 2I positions with 2 instead of 2 on the diagonal and 0 elsewhere. In an expression like this, the number k always means kI for the size of A.

Is (A + B)² equal to A² + 2AB + B²?

Only when AB = BA. In general (A + B)² = A² + AB + BA + B², and AB + BA is not 2AB.

h.en: 4.5 Zero products and unknown entries

body.en:
A surprise that is not a surprise

AB = O does not force A = O or B = O. Numbers behave differently: if xy = 0 then x = 0 or y = 0, but matrices can multiply to the zero matrix while both are non-zero.

Example

A =
11
11
and B =
1−1
−11
both have non-zero entries, yet AB =
00
00
.

Finding an unknown entry

  1. Multiply the matrices completely, keeping the unknown in place.
  2. Compare each entry with the given product.
  3. Solve the resulting equation, then check it in a second entry.

That check is essential: a wrong k often satisfies one entry and fails the next.

title.en: 5. Adjoint and Inverse of a 2x2 Matrix

h.en: 5.1 Determinant and adjoint of a 2x2 matrix

body.en:
Definitions

For A =
ab
cd
the determinant is |A| = ad − bc and the adjoint is adj A =
d−b
−ca
: swap the main diagonal and change the sign of the other two entries.

Worked example

A =
31
52
: |A| = 3(2) − 1(5) = 1 and adj A =
2−1
−53
. Because |A| = 1 the inverse equals the adjoint.

Why the adjoint works

Multiplying A by its adjoint always gives |A|I: the diagonal entries become ad − bc and the off-diagonal entries cancel. Dividing by |A| therefore leaves exactly I.

Common mistake

Changing the signs of the diagonal instead of the off-diagonal. Write the pattern once - keep a and d, flip b and c - and copy it every time.

h.en: 5.2 The inverse formula and the verification

body.en:
Formula

A⁻¹ = adj A ÷ |A| = (1/|A|) ×
d−b
−ca
, defined only when |A| ≠ 0.

Worked example

A =

Always verify

Multiply A by A⁻¹ and confirm that the result is I. One line of checking catches every sign slip: the top-left entry must come out as 1 and the others as 0.

Two properties worth remembering

  • (A⁻¹)⁻¹ = A
  • (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹, and the order reverses

The inverse is how a matrix is 'divided out': to solve AX = B you multiply on the left by A⁻¹, giving X = A⁻¹B.

h.en: 5.3 Reading the answer: what the inverse tells you

body.en:
Three readings

Value of |A|InverseMeaning for two equations
|A| ≠ 0existsone unique solution
|A| = 0, constants inconsistentdoes not existno solution - parallel lines
|A| = 0, rows proportionaldoes not existinfinitely many solutions

Engineering reading

A singular coefficient matrix means the equations are not independent: one of them repeats information already given. In a circuit or a truss that is the signature of a redundant or a floating element.

Common mistake

Finding |A| = 0 and then writing A⁻¹ = O. A zero determinant means the inverse does not exist, not that it is the zero matrix.

h.en: 6.1 Minors, cofactors and the 3x3 determinant

body.en:
Definitions

The minor Mᵢⱼ of an entry is the 2 × 2 determinant left after deleting its row and column. The cofactor carries the positional sign: Cᵢⱼ = (−1)^(i+j) Mᵢⱼ.

The sign board

+ − + / − + − / + − + . The sign belongs to the position, not to the number, so a negative entry inside the matrix does not change the pattern.

Worked example

A =
213
041
520
: expanding along the first row gives 2(0 − 2) − 1(0 − 5) + 3(0 − 20) = −4 + 5 − 60 = −59.

Shortcut

Expand along the row or column with the most zeros. Every zero removes a whole 2 × 2 determinant from the work.

h.en: 6.2 The adjoint of a 3x3 matrix

body.en:
Method

  1. Write the cofactor of all nine entries.
  2. Transpose that cofactor matrix - its rows become the columns of adj A.

Why the transpose

A × (transpose of its cofactor matrix) = |A|I. That identity is exactly what makes the inverse formula work, and it holds for every order.

Worked example

A =
123
014
560
has |A| = 1 and cofactor matrix
−2420−5
18−154
5−41
, so adj A =
−24185
20−15−4
−541
- the entries have moved across the diagonal.

Common mistake

Forgetting the transpose and calling the cofactor matrix the adjoint. The two are equal only when the cofactor matrix happens to be symmetric.

h.en: 6.3 The inverse of a 3x3 matrix

body.en:
Formula

A⁻¹ = adj A ÷ |A|, again only when |A| ≠ 0. Every entry of the adjoint is divided by the same number.

Worked example

A =
111
123
149
: |A| = 2 and adj A =
6−51
−68−2
2−31
, so A⁻¹ = (1/2)
6−51
−68−2
2−31
.

Work order that avoids errors

  1. Find |A| first. If it is 0, stop - there is no inverse.
  2. Build the cofactor matrix, one 2 × 2 determinant at a time.
  3. Transpose to get adj A, then divide every entry by |A|.
  4. Check one row of A × A⁻¹: it must give the matching row of I.

A 3 × 3 inverse needs nine minors, so a tidy layout on paper matters more than speed.

h.en: 6.4 Cramer's rule for two equations

body.en:
Setup

For a₁x + b₁y = c₁ and a₂x + b₂y = c₂ write D = a₁b₂ − a₂b₁, then replace the x-column by the constants to get Dₓ, and the y-column to get D_y.

x = Dₓ/D and y = D_y/D, valid only when D ≠ 0.

Worked example

x + y = 7 and 2x − y = 2: D = (1)(−1) − (2)(1) = −3, Dₓ = (7)(−1) − (2)(1) = −9, D_y = (1)(2) − (2)(7) = −12. So x = 3 and y = 4, which satisfy both equations.

Reading the three cases

D ≠ 0 gives one solution; D = 0 with Dₓ or D_y non-zero gives none; D = Dₓ = D_y = 0 gives infinitely many. The diagram shows the three pictures.

Common mistake

Replacing the wrong column. Dₓ swaps the coefficients of x, D_y swaps the coefficients of y - never the constants.

h.en: 6.5 The inverse-matrix method

body.en:
Method

Write the pair as AX = B with A the coefficient matrix, X the column of unknowns and B the column of constants. Then X = A⁻¹B.

Worked example

2x + y = 8 and x + 3y = 9: A =
21
13
has |A| = 5 and A⁻¹ = (1/5)
3−1
−12
, so X = A⁻¹B = (1/5)
3−1
−12
8
9
=
3
2
. Hence x = 3 and y = 2.

Word problems

Translate first, solve second. 'Two numbers add to 30 and differ by 8' becomes x + y = 30 and x − y = 8, which gives x = 19 and y = 11.

Which method should I use?

  • Cramer's rule is faster when you only need one unknown.
  • The inverse method is better when several right-hand sides share the same A.
  • Both need the same determinant - compute it once and reuse it.

Always substitute the answer back into the original equations; that single step converts a guess into a verified solution.

h.en: 6.6 Consistent, inconsistent and dependent equations

body.en:
Three cases from the determinant

DeterminantsNameGeometry
D ≠ 0consistent, independenttwo lines crossing at one point
D = 0, Dₓ or D_y ≠ 0inconsistentparallel lines - no solution
D = Dₓ = D_y = 0dependentthe same line twice - infinitely many

Worked example

2x + 3y = 7 with 4x + 6y = 14: the second row is twice the first, so D = 0 and Dₓ = D_y = 0 - every point of the line is a solution. Change the right side to 20 and the same left side becomes 4x + 6y = 20, so Dₓ ≠ 0 and there is no solution.

What to write in an exam

State D, then state the case by name, then give the conclusion. 'D = 0 and Dₓ ≠ 0, so the equations are inconsistent and have no solution' earns the mark; a bare 'no solution' may not.

Engineering reading

A dependent pair describes one physical law written twice; an inconsistent pair describes two laws that contradict each other - usually a sign error in the data.

q.en:
Write the order of A =
2−13
054
and state the values of a₁₃ and a₂₂.

a.en:
A has 2 rows and 3 columns, so the order is 2 × 3 and it holds 2 × 3 = 6 entries.

a₁₃ means row 1, column 3, so a₁₃ = 3.

a₂₂ means row 2, column 2, so a₂₂ = 5.

There is no a₃₁ because the matrix has only two rows.

a.en:
Both matrices are 2 × 2, so equality means each matching pair of entries is equal.

Top-left: x + 1 = 5, hence x = 4.

Bottom-right: y − 2 = 4, hence y = 6.

The other two entries are 3 = 3 and 2 = 2, which are already satisfied, so the answer is consistent.

12

Aᵀ =

General proof: (A + Aᵀ)ᵀ = Aᵀ + (Aᵀ)ᵀ = Aᵀ + A = A + Aᵀ, which is exactly the definition of a symmetric matrix.

q.en:
For what values of x is A =
x2
8x
singular?

a.en:
A square matrix is singular when its determinant is zero.

|A| = x·x − 2(8) = x² − 16. Setting x² − 16 = 0 gives x = 4 or x = −4.

So A has no inverse when x = 4 or x = −4; for every other x the inverse exists.

Note the two answers: a squared equation never gives just one root.

q.en: Decide the number of solutions for (a) 2x + 3y = 7 with 4x + 6y = 14 and (b) 2x + 3y = 7 with 4x + 6y = 20.

a.en:
(a) D = 2(6) − 3(4) = 0. Also Dₓ = 7(6) − 3(14) = 0 and D_y = 2(14) − 7(4) = 0, so every point on 2x + 3y = 7 is a solution: infinitely many.

(b) D = 0 again but Dₓ = 7(6) − 3(20) = −18 ≠ 0, so the equations contradict each other: no solution (parallel lines).

Rule: D = 0 always means the coefficient rows are proportional; the constants then decide between 'the same line' and 'parallel lines'.

q.en: What is a matrix?

a.en: A rectangular arrangement of numbers inside brackets. It has no value of its own; it is described by its order and its entries.

q.en: What does the order m × n tell you?

a.en: m rows and n columns, so the matrix holds m × n entries.

q.en: In a₂₃, which number is the row?

a.en: The first, 2. The row is always quoted before the column.

q.en: When are two matrices equal?

a.en: When they have the same order and every matching pair of entries is equal.

q.en: What is a square matrix?

a.en: One whose number of rows equals its number of columns, such as 2 × 2 or 3 × 3. Only square matrices have determinants and inverses.

q.en: Name four special square matrices.

a.en: Diagonal (zeros off the diagonal), scalar (equal diagonal entries), identity (ones on the diagonal) and zero (all entries zero).

q.en: When can two matrices be added?

a.en: Only when they have the same order; then each pair of matching entries is added.

q.en: When does the product AB exist?

a.en: When the number of columns of A equals the number of rows of B. The answer then has the rows of A and the columns of B.

q.en: Is AB equal to BA?

a.en: Usually not. Matrix multiplication is not commutative, and sometimes one of the two products cannot be formed at all.

q.en: How do you find the entry in row 2 and column 1 of AB?

a.en: Take row 2 of A and column 1 of B, multiply matching entries and add the products.

q.en: Does AB = O mean A = O or B = O?

a.en: No. Two non-zero matrices can multiply to the zero matrix; matrices have no zero-product rule.

q.en: What is the transpose used for?

a.en: To turn rows into columns. It defines symmetric matrices (Aᵀ = A) and appears in the rules (AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ.

q.en: How do you write the adjoint of a 2 × 2 matrix?

a.en: Swap the two diagonal entries and change the signs of the other two: for [a b; c d] the adjoint is [d −b; −c a].

q.en: When does a matrix have no inverse?

a.en: When its determinant is zero. Such a matrix is called singular, and A⁻¹ = adj A/|A| cannot be evaluated.

q.en: How do you check an inverse?

a.en: Multiply A by A⁻¹ in either order; the answer must be the identity matrix I.

q.en: What does the determinant of a coefficient matrix tell you?

a.en: If D ≠ 0 there is exactly one solution. If D = 0 the equations are either inconsistent (no solution) or dependent (infinitely many).

q.en: State Cramer's rule for two equations.

a.en: x = Dₓ/D and y = D_y/D, where Dₓ is formed by replacing the x-column with the constants and D_y by replacing the y-column.

q.en: Why must you check a solution in the original equations?

a.en: Because an arithmetic slip in one entry of the inverse or one determinant gives a wrong answer that still looks tidy; substitution is the only reliable check.
